speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE LATE W. ROSS MACDONALD TRIBUTE TO FORMER MEMBER AND SPEAKER
speechtext:
Order, please. Hon. members will be saddened to learn of the death this morning of a most distinguished Canadian, the Hon. W. Ross Macdonald.
Mr. Macdonald served Canada with great distinction for many years. He was a soldier in the first war, a member of this House, a minister, a senator, and finally, Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario.
The particular aspect of his work that will be remembered by this House, was his illustrious career as Speaker of the House of Commons during which time he presided over our affairs with great dignity and wisdom.
I am sure all members would wish me to convey their sympathy to members of Mr. Macdonald's family.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ADOPTION OF MEASURES TO ENSURE RECYCLING OF WASTE PAPER-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. This matter is explained in a letter to all members of parliament this week by the combined Pollution Probes of Ottawa, Nepean and Kanata. Waste paper accounts for over one third of solid waste in municipal garbage dumps at a time when there is a scarcity of solid waste sites which meet environmental standards. Newsprint consumption in Canada is roughly 66 lbs. per capita, and no more than 8 per cent waste newsprint without de-inking is recycled, and more de-inking plants are needed. The Canadian government endorses waste paper recycling as a means of conserving energy and our forests, but it has given no incentive to the paper industry to use more post-consumer waste paper in production, and it continues to overlook waste content in its paper purchases and discards 17,000 tons of waste paper every year.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That this House urge the government of Canada to adopt policies which would:
(A)	encourage industry to use greater amounts of recycled waste paper in paper production;
(B)	ensure greater use of recycled content in paper purchased for government use; and
(C)	require that government waste paper be recycled whenever possible.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED WITHDRAWAL OF PROPOSED CHANGE IN MINIMUM ATTACHMENT PERIOD-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Considering that a report from Statistics Canada produced yesterday indicates that the number of full time and part time job openings available to Canadians during the first three months of this year was only 48,100, a drop by 22 per cent from the number available at the same time last year, and considering that more than 760,000 Canadians are unemployed, and notwithstanding the support given to the government by the official spokesman for the Conservative Party for its proposed change in the Unemployment Insurance Act, which he described yesterday in the House of Commons as a small step in the right direction, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow):
That this House urges the government to withdraw its proposal to change the minimum attachment period for unemployment insurance benefits from eight weeks to twelve weeks.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REASON FOR DELAY IN REVISION OF PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PURPOSE OF CHANGE
ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REASON FOR DELAY IN REVISION OF PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PURPOSE OF CHANGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance-

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REASON FOR DELAY IN REVISION OF PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PURPOSE OF CHANGE
speechtext: And of the government.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REASON FOR DELAY IN REVISION OF PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PURPOSE OF CHANGE
speechtext:
-and, I might add, in the absence of many other ministers, I will put my question to the Acting Prime Minister.
The revisions in the price and profit regulations of the anti-inflation program, announced in the budget presentation of the Minister of Finance Tuesday night, have been described by a Montreal panel of accountants as a three page memo loaded with dynamite. Regrettably, there has been further confusion added to the question as to how the controls apply to business generally, and as the statements of the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board on Wednesday did little to clear the air, would the Acting Prime Minister make a positive contribution to public understanding of the program by telling the House why the announcement of the new regulations has been delayed until June 7 when the government supposedly knew what its intentions were in the budget? In addition, could the Acting Prime Minister inform the House whether any of these regulations will apply retroactively to pricing policies of business before May 25?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REASON FOR DELAY IN REVISION OF PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PURPOSE OF CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government made its announcement of the changes in the Anti-Inflation Board regulations as soon as a decision had been made by the cabinet. The first opportunity to make these announcements came in the budget.
The question of the applicability of these changes is to be found in the regulations themselves, and I would not presume in this House to answer the last part of the question. The purpose is to make the regulations apply in a fairer manner to all business and to buttress the efforts of the government to contain price increases.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REASON FOR DELAY IN REVISION OF PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PURPOSE OF CHANGE
speechtext: With special reference to the latter part of the Acting Prime Minister's answer to my earlier question, as the chairman of the AIB stated that the new regulations will establish the type of program which was intended in the first place, can the Acting Prime Minister tell the House exactly what the purpose of these regulatory changes is? Is it to help business, is it to clarify the program as far as business is concerned, or is it in fact to remedy the situation in the sense that the control program did not appear to be working and tighter regulations were required?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REASON FOR DELAY IN REVISION OF PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PURPOSE OF CHANGE
speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman knows-I am sure he has been following the course of events very closely; his many interventions in the House indicate that he has been-the purpose of these regulations is to make the rules with respect to prices fairer in their application as between companies of various kinds. Hon. members will recall that

there were various alternative ways of determining whether prices were within the guidelines. After review it was found more fair to apply a general rule than it was to provide for the alternatives that had previously been in effect. This is something that could only be determined by experience. The government makes no apologies for the review nor for the changes that have been made.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE NO FURTHER UNANNOUNCED CHANGES IN PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS
REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE NO FURTHER UNANNOUNCED CHANGES IN PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS
speechtext: A supplementary question. Noting that the budget speech of the Minister of Finance summarized only the highlights of the changes to the price and profit regulations, would the Acting Prime Minister assure the House that all the changes to the regulations not announced in the speech of the Minister of Finance are really consequential to the highlights, that is, that no additional major changes to the profit control procedures are lurking unannounced in the forthcoming regulations?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE NO FURTHER UNANNOUNCED CHANGES IN PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I could not give an undertaking, and I am sure it would be most inappropriate if I did, that there would not be further changes based on experience. In his speech the Minister of Finance announced the purport of the changes that are to be made. These will be spelled out in the regulations of the Anti-Inflation Board. It may be that on the basis of experience we will find it necessary to make further changes. That is to be expected and, I hope, would have the co-operation of the opposition.

subtopic: POSSIBLITY OF CHANGES IN REGULATIONS AFFECTING BANKS-REASON FOR DELAY IN REVISION OF BANK ACT
POSSIBLITY OF CHANGES IN REGULATIONS AFFECTING BANKS-REASON FOR DELAY IN REVISION OF BANK ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a final supplementary. Would the Acting Prime Minister indicate if it is planned to make any changes in the government's anti-inflation program, by regulation or otherwise, as it affects the banking community and could he indicate why the Bank Act revision has been delayed once again as indicated in the budget speech in that the Minister of Finance had indicated it would be tabled before the end of this month?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: POSSIBLITY OF CHANGES IN REGULATIONS AFFECTING BANKS-REASON FOR DELAY IN REVISION OF BANK ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said, I cannot give any undertaking about further revisions in the program. Our purpose is to bring about stability in costs and prices. We will take whatever measures appear appropriate for that purpose. It is not our desire to produce any more uncertainty than is necessary, but some changes are bound to be necessary in a program of this kind which is without precedent. It is bound to be modified as we have further experience. As for the revision of the Bank Act, the Minister of Finance has found himself otherwise engaged and it is necessary to postpone the introduction of the bill until after the end of this session.
May 28, 1976

subtopic: REASON FOR CHANGES IN PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS- EFFECT OF CHANGES ON CAPITAL FORMATION
REASON FOR CHANGES IN PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS- EFFECT OF CHANGES ON CAPITAL FORMATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Acting Prime Minister. The Minister of Finance stated that the new Anti-Inflation Board regulations were being formulated to achieve greater equity and effectiveness. Can the Acting Prime Minister explain exactly what was meant by this action, especially noting the need for expansion of business capital base?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REASON FOR CHANGES IN PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS- EFFECT OF CHANGES ON CAPITAL FORMATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, all these matters were taken into consideration when the decision was made to change the regulations. In our view they are more fair in their application to the business community as a whole. They remove anomalies that existed when there were various alternative ways of determining prices. The government is very much aware of the necessity of promoting capital investment and in our judgment these regulations are fair and equitable and will not interfere with the expansion of business.

subtopic: REASON FOR CHANGES IN PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS- EFFECT OF CHANGES ON CAPITAL FORMATION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Reports from the business community indicate that the capital base of business has been seriously eroded by inflation with only the government gaining. Can the minister advise if the government has studied the effects on the formation of the capital base of the change in the base period profit average from 95 per cent to 85 per cent, coupled with high interest rates? Have they studied the effect of this on the formation of capital which is required to expand business to offset inflation? Will that study be tabled? I think it is very important.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REASON FOR CHANGES IN PRICE AND PROFIT REGULATIONS- EFFECT OF CHANGES ON CAPITAL FORMATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has said, inflation is causing disruption. The purpose of the government's policy is to stop inflation and, if it is necessary, to take unusual action. If the hon. gentleman is suggesting it is more important to achieve some other objective, I do not agree with that.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED WITHDRAWAL OF PROPOSED CHANGE IN MINIMUM ATTACHMENT PROVISION-REQUEST FOR FREE VOTE ON PROPOSED CHANGE

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. I am sure we are all pleased to learn that the air traffic controllers and Treasury Board have reached agreement on the outstanding issues involving the air traffic controllers' dispute.

speechtext: Will the minister tell the House what assurance he has given the air traffic controllers that there will be no extension of bilingual air-ground communications until the commissioner of the inquiry has presented his report to the government and the report is made public?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ASSURANCES GIVEN AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS NO EXTENSION OF BILINGUAL AIR-TO-GROUND COMMUNICATIONS PENDING REPORT OF INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in addition to some explanatory changes in the terms of reference, we have reached considerable agreement about the satisfactory progress that has been made on bilingual air traffic service in the five airports where it was first introduced, that the introduction would go on progressively at Val d'Or and Bagotville, that the air advisory radio service for VFR would continue to move forward, that the use of French in emergency situations would be permitted as under the current rules and that the commission work would go forward. We would not undertake any further introduction of bilingualism until after the commission has reported and the report has been made public, except with the agreement of the controllers and Transport Canada. I put it that way because we have found that a good deal of progress can be made by sitting down together and continuing to assure everyone that safety is our prime consideration and, when procedures are available which allow the introduction of the two languages with safety, they will go forward.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: ALLEGED PROPOSAL TO REMOVE RAPESEED FROM CROWSNEST PASS RATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. All of us are very pleased that this week he inaugurates "Canada on the Move". I would like to get him on the move with reference to removing rapeseed from being within the purview of the Crowsnest Pass agreement. All over western Canada there is strong complaint about this. I bring this to his attention and ask him whether he still intends to remove rapeseed, which my administration brought under or supported under the provisions of the Crowsnest Pass rate. Is he going to stubbornly stay with his present stand and lose western Canadian farmers millions of dollars?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLEGED PROPOSAL TO REMOVE RAPESEED FROM CROWSNEST PASS RATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. I am delighted that the right hon. member has given me this opportunity to make clear that I have no proposal to put before anyone to move rapeseed away from the Crowsnest rate.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED PROPOSAL TO REMOVE RAPESEED FROM CROWSNEST PASS RATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLEGED PROPOSAL TO REMOVE RAPESEED FROM CROWSNEST PASS RATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
My specific decision has been to indicate to the Canadian Transport Commission that they ought not to charge more than the compensatory rate, which is well below cost, on rapeseed oil. However, I did point out to the western premiers when they objected to that, that at that rate oil is at a higher cost, even though below cost, than shipping rapeseed. They asked for equity between oil and rapeseed. I asked them to state clearly whether what they meant was an additional subsidy on rapeseed oil instead of hiding behind the word "equity". I got some kind of a reply to the effect that they want equity but not subsidies and,
May 28, 1976

therefore, I am no further ahead. The dilemma is there. The low rate creates distortions. There is no doubt about the fact that with rapeseed at the low rate and oil at the high rate, there is a disincentive to processing in the west just as there is in the case of feed grain and meat, because of the discrepancy between the rates on those products. Those in the west have to face up to that situation in a very realistic manner. I ask them to do so clearly and honestly, instead of hiding behind generalizations that are meaningless.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED PROPOSAL TO REMOVE RAPESEED FROM CROWSNEST PASS RATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I can only designate the minister's reply as an oily one. I ask him specifically: can he give an assurance that there will be no removal of rapeseed from the Crowsnest Pass freight statute? That is all I want to know, not this mass of words by way of explanation. Are we in Western Canada to be able to say that the minister from Saskatchewan is going to protect a major industry in our province?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLEGED PROPOSAL TO REMOVE RAPESEED FROM CROWSNEST PASS RATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
I think my previous answer said exactly what I wanted to say and what I meant to say in that regard. I think I can say it would be impossible for me to see how we could justify asking the taxpayer to pay an additional part of the cost of the movement of either meat or rapeseed products from the prairies, even though that cost may be related to a rate which is compensatory and therefore not fully cost covering. I therefore say to the right hon. gentleman that there is a real challenge facing him and those in the West who have favoured the Crow as a low rate on grain to recognize that that will be a discouragement to processing there.
About a year and a half ago I said in Edmonton that while I would fight to try to preserve the benefit of the Crow rate I thought the farmers would be better off if they got the benefit of that rate in some other way, equally assured. I made that statement without having received the approval of my colleagues in the government for any such change; no such change has been put before them. I was, in effect, making an offer to the West about what I would try to fight for for the good of the West, hoping I could persuade my colleagues. But up to this point I have not been able to get the support from the West in favour of something which would, in my view, be extremely good for the West. I wish the politicians out there would recognize that now.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED PROPOSAL TO REMOVE RAPESEED FROM CROWSNEST PASS RATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLEGED PROPOSAL TO REMOVE RAPESEED FROM CROWSNEST PASS RATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Listening to the minister's answer, it is very clear that out go the rights of the western farmer growing rapeseed to be protected under the Crowsnest Pass Agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLEGED PROPOSAL TO REMOVE RAPESEED FROM CROWSNEST PASS RATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
The interesting thing, of course, is that there has been some growing realization in the West of the nature of this problem. Just recently I had the support of the Government of Alberta for the proposition that the Crow rate on domestic grain ought not to be continued because it discourages the production of meat in Alberta and is seriously to the disadvantage of Alberta. So at least some Conservatives in one province seem to know what the facts are, though I am not sure they all do.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FREE VOTE ON PROPOSED CHANGES IN ACT-REASON FOR PROPOSED CHANGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Acting Prime Minister. In view of the statements made by Liberal backbenchers from Newfoundland-for Gander-Twillingate, Bonavista-Trini-ty-Conception, Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, from the member representing the New Brunswick constituency of Gloucester and by the hon. member from Cornwall, speaking on television last night, raising serious objections to the proposal with regard to lengthening the working period before people can qualify for unemployment insurance benefits, would the hon. gentleman assure members of the House and back bench members of his own party in particular that on this question, when the vote is taken, they will be given the right to a free vote?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FREE VOTE ON PROPOSED CHANGES IN ACT-REASON FOR PROPOSED CHANGES
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. I cannot give that assurance. When the legislation comes forward the government will take full responsibility. I hope the hon. member, when he is dealing with this subject, will bear in mind what the Minister of Finance said and what the Minister of Manpower and Immigration said, that the government's purpose would be to compensate for any particular disadvantages which might arise in any particular area of the country by a program of employment. I hope he agrees that this would be better than receiving unemployment insurance.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FREE VOTE ON PROPOSED CHANGES IN ACT-REASON FOR PROPOSED CHANGES
speechtext: Would the minister tell us why the government insists on coming forward with this proposal in the light of the fact that organizations such as the Economic Council have made it very clear that measures of this kind are counter-productive and that what is needed is not a clamping down on unemployment insurance but a massive job creation program involving expenditure in the neighbourhood of a billion dollars?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FREE VOTE ON PROPOSED CHANGES IN ACT-REASON FOR PROPOSED CHANGES
speechtext: While the government has not gone as far as the Economic Council has advised, we are moving in that direction and that is one of the purposes of the new policy which has been announced-to endeavour, by creating useful works of social value, to replace the benefits of unemployment insurance by wages.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will no doubt recall that approximately one year ago
May 28, 1976

parliament enacted Bill S-9, an act designed to repeal the Propriety or Patent Medicine Act. The PPM Act, as it is commonly termed, has served Canada well for over half a century, but certain of its provisions-notably, that relating to the secrecy of the ingredients contained in patent or proprietary medicines-were considered anachronistic.
Accordingly, Bill S-9 provided for repeal of the PPM Act effective July 1, 1976, with control of proprietary or patent medicines then to be carried out under the Food and Drugs Act and regulations. Royal assent for Bill S-9 was received on April 24, 1975. On the basis of the best information available then, it was believed that the period of time allowed to both industry and the provinces was adequate to ensure the orderly transition from control over proprietary medicines under the PPM Act to the Food and Drugs Act.
During the intervening period, industry has found considerable manufacturing difficulty in achieving the necessary labelling changes in order to meet the July 1, 1976, deadline. Problems related to the availability of labels, the need to have new registration numbers and adequate production lead time have created a situation whereby manufacturers of proprietary medicines have advised the government that they would be unable to continue having their products available to the general public unless the date of repeal was extended.
There are various classes of drug products and differing legislation controlling their sale. Prescription drugs may only be sold on the authorization of a prescription issued by a practitioner, and the medication can only be sold in pharmacies. Non-prescription drugs may be sold without the authorization of a practitioner, and by virtue of provincial legislation, non-prescription drugs not presently registered under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act can only be sold in drugstores or pharmacies. By virtue, also, of provincial legislation, exemptions are made for proprietary medicines presently registered under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act so that they may be sold in non-pharmacy outlets. In consultation with the provinces, there has been general agreement that the public should continue to have access to products for the self-medication of the symptoms of minor, self-limiting ailments.
Repeal of the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act requires, therefore, that the provinces amend provincial pharmacy legislation to refer not to the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act but to proprietary medicines in division 10 of the Food and Drugs Act and regulations. The federal government, based on assurances at the official level, had expected that the necessary changes in provincial legislation would be undertaken in time to accommodate the change in federal legislation. Some of the provinces have not as yet made the changes necessary to permit the sale of these products as proprietary medicines. Barring unforeseen circumstances, it is expected that all the required changes in provincial legislation will be enacted by the proposed repeal date of April 1, 1977.
These two factors make it necessary to extend the repeal date. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, there would develop a situation in which the general public, after July 1-which is only one month away-could not legally obtain products
Patent Medicines and Trade Mark for self-medication to which they have normally turned for treatment of minor ailments such as headaches, indigestion and other symptoms of minor disorders. The bill before this House today is designed to ensure that there is an orderly and appropriate transition period in which continuity of availability of proprietary medicines is assured.

It now appears that was not the case, for we are dealing with the same bill again. We have to ask ourselves why this is necessary and, Mr. Speaker, we can come to only one conclusion: the gross incompetence of this government or at least its arrogance and failure adequately to consult with the drug manufacturers.
I am sure some information must have been available about how long it would take to change the labelling and get new materials printed. On the basis of the general behaviour and attitude of this government, I am inclined to think there was no real consultation with the drug manufacturers a year ago which would have enabled the government to make a better prognostication of the time required. We have seen this attitude in its dealings with the provinces in the past.
The parliamentary secretary carefully worded his comments so as not to say whether there had been consultations with the provinces when the bill was first proposed and passed a year ago, or whether there has been consultation now. He said he has reason to believe it will be ready by April 1, but did not say that he had consulted the provinces and did not give any assurance that April 1 is a satisfactory date. On the basis of the government's past performance, we cannot tell that it is a suitable date. There is no evidence that the drug manufacturers will be ready by then, or that the provinces will have amended their pharmacy acts by that time.
Before passing this legislation we would need to get some assurances from the people involved so that next April we will not, again, find ourselves pressured to pass all stages in a matter of two or three seconds. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING SECURITY PROGRAM TO BE CARRIED OUT BY FOREIGN CARRIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps at the outset I might usefully touch sketch the gist of this legislation. May I say that we appreciate the co-operation of hon. members in expediting consideration of this bill. Hopefully, we shall finish all stages by one o'clock.
Canada has been one of those countries which has expressed growing concern about the threat to international air transportation posed by unlawful interference with civil aviation. This concern is, of course, heightened by the approach of the summer Olympics in Montreal and the UN conference on human settlements which is just beginning in Vancouver.
A security program for civil aviation in Canada has been developed over the past few years in co-operation with air carriers. This program follows closely the standards and recommended practices for the protection of civil aviation as set out in annex 17 of the International Civil Aviation Organization. It began with the amendment of part 5 of the Aeronautics Act which was passed in the House of Commons on July 27, 1973.
In effect, the Aeronautics Act now authorizes the governor in council to make regulations requiring the owners or operators of aircraft registered in Canada to establish, maintain and carry out such security measures as may be prescribed by the regulations. Accordingly, regulations have been enacted imposing the obligation of security measures on the owners and operators of aircraft registered in Canada. The act, however, does not authorize
May 28, 1976

regulations which would impose the obligation of similar security measures to be established and carried out by foreign air carriers operating into and out of aerodromes in Canada.
Under the present wording of the act, security measures in respect of flights by foreign air carriers from aerodromes in Canada can only be established and carried out by the Ministry of Transport itself, the result being that Canadian air carriers are burdened with the expense of establishing and carrying out their own security measures, while the Ministry of Transport must bear the burden of establishing and the expense of carrying out security measures in respect of passengers departing Canada with foreign air carriers. This is, obviously, somewhat discriminatory.
In addition, the absence of security measures by foreign air carriers transporting passengers into aerodromes in Canada is of considerable importance as many European countries do not screen passengers or goods leaving their country by aircraft. The coming international events in Canada point out the necessity of requiring foreign air carriers operating into aerodromes in Canada to adopt a security program in respect of all passengers and goods intended to be carried into and out of aerodromes in this country.
The amendments to section 5(1) as proposed in Bill S-34 are to clarify the authority to require all owners and operators of aircraft, whether registered in Canada or otherwise, to comply with security regulations in respect of flights into or out of Canadian aerodromes. The foreign air carriers would be required to use security measures equivalent to those now followed by Canadian air carriers. As I have said, the operators of Canadian registered aircraft are now required to comply with security regulations at their own expense, whereas foreign air carriers are not so required. The amendment would correct that situation.
The amendments also authorize the Ministry of Transport to institute, on its own, security measures at airports applicable to all carriers, both domestic and foreign. This would enable the ministry to impose charges for any such security services provided. If this service had to be provided without a charge to the carriers, the cost to the department is estimated at approximately $200,000 annually. This provision would only be used on the failure, particularly of foreign air carriers, to adopt a security system equivalent to that used by Canadian air carriers.
The amendments also make it an offence for a foreign-registered aircraft to land at an aerodrome in Canada without having subjected its passengers to security measures equivalent to those followed by Canadian operators. This provision will provide a measure of enforcement. It would, perhaps, be interesting for the House to note that over the past year the government of the United States has similarly moved in this direction through its anti-hijacking act of 1974 and subsequent regulations which came into effect on October 9, 1975.

We wish to voice our reservations about this aspect as we think security is, and has always been, the responsibility of the state. subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, I have the impression of having to fulfill a very difficult duty. It is perhaps the heaviest responsibility I have had to carry out since I had the privilege to attend the debates of this House and to represent a federal constituency.
In my opinion, it is extremely important to know the environment in which I live and the category of citizens I represent in this House to understand the way I intend to fulfil my responsibility. It is also important that hon. members be aware that my constituents are largely workers. Most of my electors are honest people who work for two large companies, Alcan and Price. The other citizens are small businessmen and I must unfortunately point out that I have to face extremely difficult social conditions because the unemployment rate is 20 per cent and because a large number of citizens, far too many, are poor.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the decision I have to make today must be based on the mandate I received on the category of people who will be affected by our decision. How can the death penalty influence those people who gave me the terms of reference to represent them? Mr. Speaker, a few years ago already I had the opportunity to take a particular interest in that extremely important debate on capital punishment. On many occasions I met citizens from all walks of life. I discussed with them. I explained to them that the decision I had to make should not be emotional; in other words, I should try not to make a decision after reading newspapers featuring a sordid crime committed the day before, I should try not to react when meeting a group of people who are in an emotional state of mind, which is quite understandable sometime, because of a tragedy some place in this country.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, one also has to recognize that with such an important decision, my personal opinion should not prevail. It is known and admitted-and I never hesitated to say so-that I never believed violence could solve any sort of problem, either in my family or in my province, my country or within the government. It is a stand that I am prepared to take any time, anywhere and in anyone's presence.
However, as I have said, this personal opinion does not necessarily reflect the decision I must take.
Mr. Speaker, in order to make a valid, thoughtful and responsible decision I should not follow an emotional reaction of mine nor my own view on this matter.
Above all, I must ask myself where lies the real interest of all the citizens I represent in this House and how I can uphold and protect it. Mr. Speaker, I feel that the only way to deal with the issue of capital punishment is to consider scientifically the effects of its retention or its abolition. Indeed, one cannot overemphasize the danger of false conclusions based on of vague terms and inaccurate figures found in reports on crime, particularly when such reports can lead to changes in the policy on crime.
The five major questions which, in my opinion, should be asked and which influenced my position are the follow-

Capital Punishment
ing: first, are murders on the increase in Canada, and if so, is it due to the suspension of the death penalty? Second, is the death penalty effective as a deterrent? Third, how effective is the death penalty as a means to control and prevent crime? Fourth, what is the age and profession of the people charged or convicted of murder? Finally, the fifth question, what relationship is there between murderers and their victims?
Is it necessary, Mr. Speaker, to specify that the problem of capital punishment will not be solved, I admit, only through scientific research with moral and theological aspects related to the only basic question: Is life the most precious of all possessions? Does society have the right to take it away from a human being considered undeserving? Does the action of the state doing away with a criminal for good become revenge? Is it an act of violence by society against someone blamed of having been violent?
Regarding the first question, Mr. Speaker, about the impact of the increase in murders and criminality, I would like to make one point clear. Some rather interesting statistics in this regard show that the number of murders as such has increased at an average rate of 0.5. In other words, between 1965 and 1974, the average increase in murders has not been what certain people say. This average has been constant. What has gone up, though, is the number of criminal offences, and an important distinction must be made. Aggravated thefts, assaults and attempted assaults have increased. This indicates, Mr. Speaker, that violence is on the increase in our society, all forms of violence, verbal violence, written violence, violence in families, in society everywhere. This is where the real problem is. This violence, which we foster about everywhere, leads to murder. But when we want to control murder, we do not come to grips with the root of the problem but only with its head.
Mr. Speaker, the second part of the question I was asking myself a few minutes ago is this: did the abolition of the death penalty increase crime in general? I would like to remind you of a very important and useful comment of the British committee in the conclusions to its studies of the death penalty.
The general conclusion that they have reached is that, in all the figures which they have studied, there is no definite proof that the abolition of the death penalty may have led to an increase in the homicide rate or that its re-establishment may have led to a decrease.
Mr. Speaker, this brings me to study very important statistics. I do admit that statistics are not sufficient indications, but they are very useful. For example, between 1970 and 1974, a study was made in the United States in various abolitionist and non-abolitionist states. These statistics are extremely precise and interesting. You can notice than in ten abolitionist states, where the death penalty does not exist, the crime rate varies between 4.6 and 5.8 per cent, which means that it is rather low. The same study has been made in 40 non-abolitionist states, where the death penalty does exist. In these 40 states, the murder rate varies between 7.8 and 8.8 per cent. This is an indication that the death penalty has such, and this is what I assert, does not have a real effect on the crime rate. For

example, in Georgia, which is a state where the death penalty exists, the crime rate is 17.8 per cent. If we also look at the statistics in other countries of the world, we can notice, for example, that in Europe in general, the countries which have abolished the death penalty have rather low homicide or murder attempt rates. For example, among these nations are Austria, Denmark, Finland, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom. This means, Mr. Speaker, that we should not be mistaken about the real significance of the death penalty.
The second question is: is the death penalty a useful deterrent. The arguments of those who claim that the death penalty has a deterrent effect are usually based on common sense rather than on empirical data, for these data tend to the contrary. Schuster asserted that the statistical studies always came to the conclusion that the death penalty has no important deterrent effect and that the relative frequency of murders in a given population depends on the cultural conditions in which this population lives.
The proponents of the death penalty claim that it is the most powerful of deterrents. They reason this way because of the fear that can influence human behaviour. This reasoning is based on the theory that when man can predict the consequences of his actions, he will deliberately choose between two opposite behaviour patterns and that personal reward will be the criterion of his choice. Schuster notes that such a conclusion is not in accordance with modern psychology and sociology that believe that human behaviour, far from being calculated and conscious, obeys to a large extent to habits and inspiration of the moment.
I also have here a very interesting quotation from Dr. Roche: "The argument that the death penalty intimidates criminals can be valid to the extent that it is based on the hypothesis of a state of mind that we imagine to be unchanging, but experience has shown rather that a given community always includes a group of people with criminal tendencies which transcend the intimidating effect of any penalty."
The argument of retentionists gives much too much importance to the power of fear. Fear does not prevent people from doing what they want, Mr. Speaker. The attraction of immediate pleasure wins easily over the far away possibility of death. We must not forget that the life of everybody involves all sorts of risks. You can be injured or killed by a car or killed accidentally in certain professions like the mining or construction industries.
The threat of lung cancer does not stop our friends from smoking. Certain people drink themselves to death or entertain other vices which will cause their downfall. In one word, Mr. Speaker, to shorten my comments, which I now find are taking more time than I had expected, I shall simply say that deterrence, in my opinion, is not a factor in the case of the great majority of criminals in our society, since, and those are the last two questions that I want to answer, how are murders committed and by whom?
Mr. Speaker, the one thing that should not be overlooked is that statistics on murder include those committed by the underworld, by people who believe that violence is the answer. There are also murders committed by mentally ill people, those committed on impulse; the latter make up the
May 28, 1976

greatest number of murders. Statistics indicate that 70 per cent of murders in Canada are committed by people who know one another through a financial, romantic or any other type of relationship.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, in considering the way murders are committed in Canada we must conclude that if the death penalty were enforced, it would not apply in most cases, it would apply only in 2 or 3 per cent of cases.
I am not coming to my main argument. What type of people commit murders in our Canadian society?
If we examine the statistics, Mr. Speaker, we note that 50 per cent of murders in Canada are committed by workers, by those who are in difficult social circumstances, who have been living in a divided family, in a climate of uncertainty and affliction and who are left alone, when their parents are divorced, or drunkards, people who have not assumed their responsibilities. Those people now commit murders in society.
Let us examine the list of murderers. People like Cotroni and Obront who have some standing never appear on the list of murderers. Is it because those individuals are more intelligent than others? No. It is because they were given some advantage by society, because their living conditions were more normal and their education, training and their circumstances did not prompt them to commit reprehensible acts.
Mr. Speaker, the death penalty is an action taken against the worker, the underprivileged, the one who does not have a lawyer competent enough to get him a fair trial, to defend him and get him out of trouble. As concerns the worker, whatever the seriousness of his crime he is unable to defend himself. The punishment is unfair as it is never applied in a rational, real and fair way. This measure is against workers and in a riding where most people are workers I shall never accept to vote for a measure which is against the majority of the people. I think I have to make those people understand that if I vote for that kind of measure I vote against their interests.
I recognize that there are sordid crimes. I recognize that we all have the same reaction: let us eliminate those people. But who are they? They live in difficult circumstances. Criminals are created by society, by everyone of us. There should not be scapegoats of our own mistakes in every field.
I wish to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying this: as a member of the House of Commons I think I have the responsibility of not choosing the easy way out, not following the trend before people whose first reaction is often to say: We want capital punishment! My duty is to explain to those people that we must help each other-eliminate crime, we must help the less privileged, people with problems and not depend only on government legislation. Every individual at any level from any government on any side of this House, whether man, woman, professional or worker, is part of a big family and we are all responsible for each others' actions.
I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that this legislation will be passed. However I am a Democrat and what ever the result I shall be ready to accept it. But I am convinced that if we provide stricter measures to go with capital punishment, because if there were no strict measures going with it I
Capital Punishment
would not agree, as criminals can be released in the streets after two or three years and the people are very concerned and that is what they want. We should not necessarily take the life of those individuals but they should be excluded from society long enough to pay for their mistakes.
Mr. Speaker, I close on this wish: I trust that, regardless of the result of the vote, we will understand that the real interest of the citizens lies in the fact that we work with them, for them, by placing at their disposal all our resources as members of Parliament, to help them solve the basic problems; when those problems no longer exist, I expect that the crime rate we deplore at this time will have lessened considerably. At least, that is the hope I cherish. I offer all those who want to work with me towards that ideal-I know they are the vast majority if not all hon. members-my co-operation. As for me, I am willing to help them, that we might truly help the people in the right sense of the word.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that I will abide by what most hon. members have been saying at the beginning of their speeches, and that is to be brief. My intention is to be brief because practically everything that has to be said has been said in this debate. However, I think it is essential that on issues such as this members of parliament go on record so that their constituents will have an opportunity to judge their stand, because this is an extremely important issue. It is not an issue upon which parties can take a stand, but we as individual members will have a free vote, or a supposedly free vote. I hope to speak a little more about that later in my remarks. Let me state at the beginning that while I believe in capital punishment for all premeditated murder or planner murder, which makes up approximately 1 per cent of the murders committed, I also believe a more humane form of execution should replace hanging.
Violent crime in Canada increased 90 per cent in the ten-year period 1965 to 1974, and the murder rate doubled in that same period of time. In 1965 there were 243 murders, and in 1974 there were 545 murders. As I stated, the murder rate doubled in that period of time from 1.2 per
100,000	population to 2.4 per 100,000 population. Despite the fact that 38 policemen and prison guards were murdered in this same ten-year period, no convicted murderer has been executed. In essence, what we have had for a number of years is the abolition of capital punishment, and the murder rate has doubled.
Evidence is inconclusive as to whether capital punishment is a deterrent. Any discussion of the merits or otherwise of capital punishment goes beyond the area of politics and each person makes up his own mind according to the dictates of his conscience and his judgment. It has also been shown that few people will change their mind or their opinion as a result of reading statistics, studies or reports on this subject; and the shame of it is that far too often we, as individuals, are concerned with justifying our own reasoning when we should be searching for a just reason.
The abolitionists claim that capital punishment is not deterrent to would-be murderers. In my opinion this is an empty argument and completely beside the point. There is

May 28, 1976
Capital Punishment
no way to determine how many murders were not committed by those who wanted to commit the act but did not for fear of execution. The question should be, does the supreme crime demand the supreme penalty? In effect, do we place the highest possible value on the life of the victim?
The abolitionists say capital punishment has no deterrent effect. There are no facts to prove it one way or the other. But to say that the death penalty is no deterrent is to say that men do not fear death, and I find that to be a rather incredible assertion. Fear of death, in my view, is an instinctive reaction. I ask, how many of us in this chamber do not value or fear for our lives? Life is regarded by man as a precious possession which he wishes to preserve more eagerly than anything else. He would therefore defend it to the utmost against every threat, including the threat of capital execution. Every such threat arouses his fear, and as a rational being he would try to conduct himself in such a manner that that threat would be avoided. It is assumed that the potential threat is made vivid to him by the fact that he knows the death penalty exists. If capital punishment is never carried out, it loses its deterrent effect. There must be a serious and real risk of execution for the death penalty to be an effective tool, because crime will not decrease until being a criminal becomes more dangerous than being a victim.
In my view, fear of death is an instinctive reaction, and to conquer or subdue that fear is a feat some people are not capable of. In wartime, fear of death operates on the battlefield itself. No one who has seen death in its many forms can say, and be believed, that fear of death is not a powerful factor in determining any course of action.
The abolitionists usually state as an argument in favour of abolition that a mistake can be made in carrying out capital punishment. Although this is a valid comment, it is not a valid argument in a debate on capital punishment, because what we are discussing now is what the price should be for an individual who commits premeditated or planned murder. We are not arguing or discussing the merits of our judicial system. If there are errors in that area, they must be safeguarded against; but that statement is not a valid argument in this debate because, as I said, what we have to resolve here is what to do with individuals who have been found guilty of taking another individual's life intentionally.
The very individuals we ask to give us protection deserve protection themselves. If what is known as capital punishment today is done away with, they will have no protection. What will a criminal imprisoned for life have to lose if he kills a prison guard? In reality, he will gain his freedom if his bid for escape succeeds; if it does not, he has lost nothing if capital punishment is done away with, even though he has killed a prison guard.
I believe it is the prime duty of the government to offer its citizens protection against violent crime, and in my view capital punishment is a necessary tool to ensure this protection.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I wish to register a few other comments. There was a debate on capital punishment in my constituency in which I participated. Assisting the

stand on retention was an extremely capable man, Tom Forgrave, the city's intergovernmental officer, while Edmonton lawyer, Robert Newton and the Reverend George Rodgers of Sherwood Park United Church supported the abolitionist view. A vote was taken from the audience before the debate began, and again afterwards, and I should like to record it in Hansard. The meeting was sponsored by the Pembina Federal Association Zone Two of the Progressive Conservative party. An audience poll showed 35 in favour of retention, 20 for abolition, and 17 undecided. Two hours later, after the debate, 37 backed the death penalty, 7 were still undecided and 27 favoured abolition.
I should like to pay tribute to the individuals who debated for abolition, Mr. Speaker, for, as the figures show, they gained votes in this debate. It is also noteworthy that in a questionnaire I sent out to the constituency in the fall of 1975, the results showed that 6 per cent of those who returned the questionnaire were in favour of abolition, 20 per cent were in favour of the law as it now stands and 74 per cent were in favour of capital punishment for premeditated murder. A report of the meeting I referred to previously appeared in the Edmonton Journal and referred to Mr. Forgrave's participation as follows;
"My father tells me-Canadian people-are generally right" on social issues, Mr. Forgrave said. That's why there is such massive support for the death penalty at this time.
Mr. Forgrave said capital punishment is "almost always more humane" than capital murder. "Somehow or other there has to be a way of dealing with premeditated murder," especially of policemen and prison guards", he said.
My sentiments are very much the same, Mr. Speaker. When I hear members of this House debating on the side of abolition, I am puzzled to know what makes them think their individual conscience is so much wiser than the collective conscience of their constituents. I think far too many members are trying to hedge their bets by taking both sides of the argument so that they can send something out to their constituents which will make good reading for both points of view.
I have personally found this to be a very trying issue, as I am sure all hon. members have; I must commend my colleague and good friend, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche), for making his views known in this debate. I can imagine how trying it must have been for him, and when I compare it with my own experience, I respect him all the more.
Yesterday the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston) said that in reality there will not be a free vote in this chamber. I am inclined to agree with him. I have the record of the last three times this matter came before the House and have examined the voting pattern of some members. There is one member, now in the cabinet, who voted for retention in the past. If members opposite are ambitious and wish to gain a place in the cabinet, I suggest they vote for abolition-the possibility of a reten-tionist gaining admittance into the cabinet is very slim.
It will be of particular interest to see how the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Lessard), the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, votes. In the previous three debates he voted for retention each time. Now he is a member of the cabinet. Did he have to sell his soul to receive that position?
