speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a member of Parliament does not often have the opportunity to take part in such an emotional and attention-getting debate as the one on Bill C-84.
Is it any wonder, since everyday some media feature the most loathsome and sordid crimes. As a result, many people feel that our society does not know any other law than the law of the jungle and that only stronger action on the part of the government would bring criminals to their senses. No one can deny that our country is going through an unprecedented crime wave. One needs only mention that violent crimes of all kinds have increased by 90 per cent in the past 10 years. As regards the worst of all crimes, murder, its rate has gone from one per 100,000 in 1961 to 2.4 in 1974.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that Canadians are justified in calling for strong government action in order to stop such raving madness. That is precisely what this government
Capital Punishment
intends to do and after close consideration, I cannot but agree with the plan of action they are submitting to Parliament and the Canadian people for this purpose.
Many Canadians think that the retention of capital punishment is essential to public security. I can understand myself their position because sometimes some murders are so revolting as to prompt us to seek a revenge that would probably be as cruel as the murder itself. It is precisely this public indignation at the vileness of some homicides which explains why a large number of Canadians would be in favour of the death penalty, according to public opinion polls. However, I do not think that the legislators' decision in this regard should be influenced by such feelings. Mr. Speaker, in this case it would be too easy for a member of parliament to hide behind the results of public opinion polls in order to evade his responsibilities.
Indeed, his first duty is to see that his constituents are well informed of the intentions of the government and then to explain to them why the government deems advisable to take such action and try to meet their objections. It is only after having exhausted all those means that a member of parliament can really come to the conclusion that his constituents are against the bill.
Shortly after the law and order program was introduced in this House February last, I sent to all residents in my constituency the main lines of Bills C-83 and C-84, urging them to tell me about the changes they favoured. Furthermore, I invited them to public meetings which actually took place in March and April, so that each and everyone could make their views known on the subject. Following those consultations, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the people first want the government to wage an all-out war against crime and they accept that the death penalty be replaced by life imprisonment provided the Parole Board does its work seriously and competently.
Mr. Speaker, nothing illustrates more the will of the government to ensure the security of all the people than the 27 per cent increase this year in the estimates for the federal administration of justice-from $61 million to $78 million. That such a substantial increase should be provided at the very time when the federal government must resort to severe budgetary cut backs is the best proof that law and order is a vital concern of this government.
But is it true to say that peace and security will be more easily protected if we retain capital punishment? Reten-tionists believe that the death penalty is a deterrent which can bring a potential murderer back to better feelings. It goes without saying that I would unconditionally support the retention of that penalty if it had been shown that the fear of death really deterred murderers from committing their crime. Now, there is no evidence that such is the case.
Mr. Speaker, in 1962, a total of 11 policemen on duty were killed, even though at that time the death penalty was in force and in spite of the fact that during that year two hangings took place in Canada. In 1975, only two policemen we killed on duty although for all practical purposes capital punishment was abolished during the last few years, since the cabinet systematically commuted death sentences into life imprisonment.
And what about the fact that in 1974, Mr. Speaker, the ten American states that abolished the death penalty had a

May 28, 1976
Capital Punishment
homicide rate of 5.81 per 100,000 population while that of the retentionists states was 8.85? Mr. Speaker, the case is often mentioned of the two criminals who, having kidnapped someone in an American abolitionists state, crossed two other abolitionists states to finally end up by killing their victim in New Hampshire where capital punishment still applied and where in fact they were condemned to death.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, whoever is familiar with the workings and officials in the world of justice and its courts, knows that the individual stands a chance of being found guilty if the possibility of the death penalty is not there to influence the decision of the jury. So, as noticed in Great Britain, after abolition of the death penalty the number of accused found mentally unsound decreased considerably. We must therefore conclude that before abolition juries were more inclined to find a murderer insane and thus spare him the supreme penalty. It would also seem that the existence of capital punishment too often inhibits punishment of the murderer at the hands of the law.
We also know that a large number of Canadian police officers oppose abolition because they feel retention will mean less danger in their work. Quite the contrary, I believe that a murderer will be much less reluctant to kill a policeman attempting to arrest him, if he knows that his earlier murder entails death anyway. In other words, that murderer has nothing to lose, he is facing the same ultimate penalty no matter how many murders he commits.
Mr. Speaker, we must also remember that our system of justice is not above error, that the risk of judicial errors can never be totally eliminated. No one has forgotten the case of Wilbur Coffin who was hanged in 1956, although in the eyes of many his guilt was never clearly established. Similarly, there was the case in Alberta of Raymond Cooke, who was executed in 1960, although his guilt has been seriously questioned since then. For these reasons, it is not sensible in my view to retain such an irreversible punishment, which has never been proved to deter potential murderers anyway.
Abolition is so much the more acceptable that Bill C-84 substitutes punitive measures that should adequately protect society. It does not seem to me that many Canadians believe life imprisonment does not protect society as much as capital punishment. However, many want safeguards, in the fear that the National Parole Board may show unwarranted clemency. Bill C-84 provides that an individual convicted of planned and deliberate murder, or of the killing a police officer or a prison or penitentiary employee is eligible for parole after 25 years' imprisonment.
Under the new legislation, when reviewing parole applications the National Parole Board will be bound to invite to its proceedings two citizens from the area concerned who will be entitled to vote and will be chosen among local policemen, municipal executives or professional or business association members. The board will then be able to rely on sensible advice from people representative of the local community, who are especially concerned about their fellow citizens' security. The contribution of those people, deep-rooted in their community and

known for their good judgment, should eliminate to a large extent the errors of judgment too often made by the board and allow the latter to regain the confidence of the population.
Mr. Speaker, the act also provides that an individual condemned to life imprisonment may, after serving 15 years, ask three judges of a superior court to declare him eligible for parole. One can assume that such applications will only be agreed upon in exceptional cases. Be that as it may, the National Parole Board may still deny parole even though the applicant has been declared eligible by the court.
Mr. Speaker, I think the legislation should have provided for parole. Indeed, we should not refuse any hope to the inmate who sincerely wishes to get rehabilitated and whose goodwill is above suspicion. Moreover, such provision should encourage prisoners to behave correctly and this in turn would appreciably reduce the violence which may be directed against prison guards and prison staff in general. One must keep in mind indeed that the proposed legislation provides that any remission will have to be deserved through model behaviour. Thus the prisoner will keep hoping to be released before the end of his sentence if he behaves decently during his imprisonment. In refusing him such a hope, the inmate would have nothing else to loose and could become dangerous for his guards and the prison staff.
Mr. Speaker, one often hears that it would be better to execute murderers rather than keep them at the expense of the taxpayers at an estimated annual cost of $14,000. It should be pointed out, I think, that this is the average cost per prisoner, including the fixed costs of the overall operation of penitentiaries. But, those fixed costs would not be reduced at all if the 13 people now on death row in federal penitentiaries were executed tomorrow morning. In fact, studies have shown that the marginal or additional annual cost incurred for the presence of each of the 13 prisoners in Canadian penitentiaries is about $1,300.
Mr. Speaker, some retentionists like to quote from the Bible to support their position. I would like to remind those people of the message of the Canadian Catholic Conference issued on January 26, 1973, in which Canadian bishops said, and I quote:
We believe it is an abuse to turn to the Bible-and particularly to the Old Testament-to justify the retention of the death penalty. The Bible where it recommends the death penalty must be analysed in the light of the historical background in which it has been written; it cannot be applied to the letter in Canada today. As a matter of fact, each of the quotations from the Old Testament must be examined in the light of the numerous parts of the New Testament where Jesus Christ condemns this habitual tendency in man to react to an insult by another insult and invites us instead to be magnanimous. Violence and hostility are not offset by measures of violence and hostility.
Furthermore, on March 4, the same group stated in a press release, and I quote:
The Board of Directors of the Canadian Catholic Conference states that it is in favour of the abolition of capital punishment in Canada and at the same time urges the government to undertake immediately the fair reforms needed in our penitentiary system and in the whole area of justice.
Mr. Speaker, I know that a number of my fellow citizens whose sincerity is beyond doubt are convinced that the well-being of our society requires the retention of capital
May 28, 1976

punishment. I urge them however to consider the arguments put forward by those who do not share their views. I want them to know especially that abolitionists want just as much as them that order prevail in our country, that violence disappear from our streets and our homes. As for me, the dictates of my conscience compel me to support Bill C-84, and I could not do otherwise.
I trust my constituents who might not agree with me on this issue, and I know that they will judge me on my parliamentary work as a whole when I stand for re-election, and not on the position I have taken during one debate, however important it might be.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say at the outset that I do not welcome participation in this debate. It is a debate which for many of us raises many questions. I recall in 1972, shortly after my election to this House, we were faced with the bill that initiated the second five-year moratorium on capital punishment, with the exception of the killing of police officers and prison guards. I recall the agony a number of us went through at that time. That agony today during this debate does not seem to be any less, especially in view of the fact that the bill now provides for the permanent abolition of the death penalty where before it was for a five-year period only.
I also recall from the 1972 debate the divisiveness that was in the House. Sad to say, I see that divisiveness, that dividing one member from another just underneath the surface in this House at the present time. While I might not agree with many people who feel that Bill C-84 warrants their support, I will respect them for their decision and for the conclusion they have drawn after, I am sure, as much soul searching as I have done.
Possibly I should give a bit of background and the reason why I have come to my conclusion. I find it somewhat difficult to begin to discuss this whole issue in view of the fact that in 1972 many of us voted for another five-year moratorium, thinking at that time the five-year period would in fact be implemented and that the government would observe the provisions of the bill it itself introduced. That has not been the case.
After but a short period of time we are now faced with an abolitionist bill. I can only conclude that in 1972 the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) was biding time in a minority House. The first five-year moratorium had ended. Knowing that complete abolition would not carry at that time, he brought in another five-year moratorium hoping that would carry in a minority House, The government, having gained a majority, we now have before us a bill to abolish capital punishment.
Looking at my participation in 1972, and again today, and also at the comments the Solicitor General made at that time, I can come to no other conclusion than that was the best he could get in 1972. He did not have any intention of finding out whether during that second five-year period capital punishment was a deterrent or not. We will now never know because since 1962 the government has chosen to commute all death sentences.
One can only conclude that the Solicitor General, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), knowing that by the end of 1977 the second
Capital Punishment
five-year moratorium would have ended and, faced with a possible general election in 1978, did not want this issue bouncing around at that time. While that might sound somewhat cynical, there may be a fair bit of truth in that statement.
There is another reason why I am somewhat cynical. We have before us the so-called peace and security package, Bills C-83 and C-84. The Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice both stated that the provisions of Bill C-83, the gun control legislation, will not reduce the incidence of crime in Canada. However, they persist in combining Bill C-83 and Bill C-84, stating that once those two bills are passed there will be peace and security on Canada's streets, and the incidence of crime, especially violent crime, will diminish. Again taking the words of the Solicitor General, that is absolutely false. He himself has said on many occasions that Bill C-83 will not affect the operations of the criminal element, so there is justification for the feelings now prevailing that the government has failed to protect society adequately. Many law-abiding citizens believe more attention is given to the person who commits a crime than to the person who suffers as a result of it.
The point which is to be made is that all of us would like to live in a society where punishment is not necessary but we just do not happen to be fortunate to live in a society of that kind. I agree that no one can prove conclusively, by using statistics, that capital punishment is a deterrent to murder. Nor for that matter can the abolitionists prove that the peace and security bills, C-83 and C-84, will act as a deterrent, though on one hand they claim that the arguments of the retentionists, who say capital punishment is a deterrent, are not valid, but on the other they claim that the longer prison sentences will be.
Up to the present the government has seen fit to commute every death sentence despite the legislation brought in by the Solicitor General in 1972 which provided for the death penalty in certain cases. What we have no means of knowing is the number of murders which would have been prevented had the death penalty been exercised. Criminals knew, and they know today, that if they are given the death sentence it will automatically be commuted. They know that in effect abolition does prevail at the present time.
One thing is crystal clear. We have seen the murder rate double over the last ten years-I am talking in terms of the rate per 100,000 of population. We know for sure that the suspension of the death penalty and its replacement by the use of the prison system has not been an effective deterrent. We know it has not reduced the incidence of murder; in fact there has been a doubling of the murder rate. As a result there is a restive mood in society; citizens feel the law has been too lax and are calling for the return of the death penalty.
Much has been said in this debate about opinion polls. I find it interesting to hear it argued that members of this House should not be influenced by the results of polls on capital punishment. Yet every four years or so we go out on the hustings to engage in what amounts to a general poll across Canada and to ask for continued support. That poll, Mr. Speaker, is a conclusive one because whoever gets

Capital Punishment
most votes is able to sit in this House and represent the people. I hear the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) mention the name of my right hon. friend from Prince Albert. I am quite sure he can speak for himself and will do so at the appropriate time.
I may say that I conducted a poll in my own riding on this question. I am not a scientific pollster but when I get a return in which 90.3 per cent are in favour of the death penalty in the case of premeditated murder I draw the conclusion that a large majority of the people in my constituency are not happy about the way in which the cabinet is commuting death sentences passed on people who have killed prison guards and police officers.
The opposition likes to portray those of us who are retentionists as being bloodthirsty, as being unsophisticated or as being less educated than others in society. I do not know how this reflects on the opinion of the electorate if the electorate is also in favour of capital punishment. No, Mr. Speaker, I believe retentionists have the same sense of responsibility as the abolitionists claim for themselves alone.
What about the length of the prison term proposed in the legislation? The bill before us would replace the death penalty with a fixed term of 25 years for first degree murder-there are provisions for parole which I shall not go into at this moment. The penalty for second degree murder is 15 years imprisonment. The question which immediately occurs to me is this: is a fixed minimum sentence less barbaric than the death sentence? What happens to a person who is placed in prison for 25 years?
We know that the rate of recidivism increases with the length of time a person is in prison. I thought I should go to an authority on this aspect so I turned to an authority the Solicitor General likes to quote-I call him the high priest of the movement in favour of abolition of capital punishment. My authority is Dr. Fattah, and I understand he did a fair amount of research for the minister before coming to the conclusion that capital punishment was not a deterrent. In an article contributed to a weekly publication put out by Simon Fraser University on March 11, he wrote:
On February 24, 1976, the Liberal government tabled one of the most retrogressive pieces of the legislation ever presented in the House of Commons-the so-called peace and security program. Abolition of capital punishment is in itself a very commendable move, a move long overdue, but substituting a mandatory life sentence with a minimum of 25 years imprisonment is, to say the least, illogical, irrational, inhuman, arbitrary and unscientific.
A minimum of 25 years creates a distinct category of men without hope and a man without hope is capable of doing anything and everything to draw attention to his cause and to his condition, as has been amply demonstrated in two recent incidents in the B.C. Penitentiary at New Westminster.
On the last page there is this paragraph:
I still remember back in January, 1973, when Marcel Prud'homme, MP for Montreal St. Denis and James Fleming, MP for York l^est, suggested that the government bill be amended to imprison killers for a minimum of 25 years. Solicitor General Warren Allmand and other members of the cabinet were the first to declare their opposition. It is disconcerting and disenchanting to see the government, after only three years, adopt the same retrogressive suggestion it once condemned.
[Mr. Epp.)
Abolitionists often say that those of us who are retentionists are swayed by opinion polls. Yet the very man who presented the background papers to the Solicitor General's peace and security package calls the bill irrational, inhumane, and uses various other appropriate expressions.
The United Church of Canada, which has taken an abolitionist stand-and I respect them for it-in a letter dated May 18, 1976, a copy of which I received on May 28, wrote to the Solicitor General and stated that the mandatory sentences were not acceptable to them. I should like to quote Nos. 5 and 13 of their reasons:
5. What happens to the inmate when he gets out of prison after serving 25 years? Most sociological data in this regard would say that the person would be more dangerous coming out than going in.
13. In your publication entitled "Highlights of the Peace and Security legislation", in the introduction on page one is the following statement: "In a society that places such a high value on the dignity of the individual the use of the death penalty must be viewed as an unacceptable and essentially purposeless form of punishment". It is our view that the proposed legislation does nothing to uplift the dignity of such individuals. We seem to be substituting one indignity for another.
The last point to be made on that sentence is that if a person who is convicted of first degree murder is placed in prison for 25 years with minimal hope, we are asking our fellow citizens, those who serve as prison guards, and other personnel in our prisons, to take care of this person. We are asking them in the course of duty to put their lives on the line, so to speak, every day because a person without hope, as it has been expressed by the various people I have quoted, is liable to engage in further killing. We are really asking prison guards to give a service well beyond that which I think should be expected of them.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, the United Church letter goes on to refer to the prison system and the negative effects that they see resulting therefrom. Let me quote reasons 4 and 12 in their letter:
4. There will be an increase in prison population and therefore increased human pressures as well as increased cost.
12. This will of course lead to far greater institutionalization of human beings who would be unable to function without the institution.
Putting those arguments aside, Mr. Speaker, the main reason that I am a retentionist is that I take a moral or theological position. In entering that argument I am not trying to say for one moment that those people who are not abolitionists do not take a moral position on which to base their argument. Neither am I saying that in their conscience they have not looked at the theological question in coming to a decision different from mine. In fact one of the best pieces of work that I have seen on this very dilemma is by Rabbi Plant of the Holy Blossom Synagogue in Toronto who, being an abolitionist, after looking at both the abolitionist and retentionist arguments, concludes that the one thing we must remember is that we come to our conclusions honestly and sincerely, and that a luxury we cannot afford is to try to say, "I am right and you are wrong".
One issue should be clarified immediately, Mr. Speaker. I do not like to get personal in this House but I feel that to a point I have to because of my background. The conclusion has been automatically drawn that I am an abolitionist. I imagine that this has given rise to certain press releases by the Canadian Council of Churches, some of which I should like to refer to briefly this afternoon. In a press release
May 28, 1976

dated January 16, 1975, a little better than a year ago, the Canadian Council of Churches stated that the Mennonite Church had taken a position on capital punishment, namely, an abolitionist position. I wrote to the Canadian Council of Churches on February 6, 1975, in response to that press release and I should like to read in part the letter I wrote to them:
While the Anabaptist view generally opposed capital punishment, most churches adhering to the concept of Anabaptist faith and, specifically, Mennonite doctrine, have not officially endorsed abolition of capital punishment. Particularly the denomination that I am a member of is divided on this issue and has not been able to formulate a policy which has widespread acceptance in our Brotherhood. Therefore, I would suggest to you that you correct the press release that you have issued with the hope that a wrong impression will not be created by the material that you have published.
Further, Mr. Speaker, I did not receive a reply to my letter. In an almost identical press release a little more than a year later, on March 2, 1976, the Canadian Council of Churches stated that certain bodies had spoken in favour of abolition of capital punishment, and they listed among them the Mennonite Church. I know this press release went to all members of parliament, obviously to create the impression among members of parliament that a number of churches, among them the Mennonite Church, were in favour of the abolition of capital punishment.
In response to that press release I wrote to the Canadian Council of Churches on March 10, 1976, and in part I said:
Further, in my letter of February 6, 1975, I stated that I found in view of the fact that your press release was incorrect that it would be in your interest to correct the false impression that you had created through the press release. Unfortunately, I have not received a reply to my letter of February 6, 1975.
In your letter of March 2, 1976, you again stated that the Mennonite Church has spoken in favour of abolition of capital punishment-no such thing has happened. Again I repeat that the General Conference of Mennonites which is but one denomination among a number of Mennonite circles has passed a resolution opposing capital punishment. While the debate on capital punishment is taking place in most Mennonite Churches as I am sure it is being carried on in other Churches, I would like to point out that your letter of March 2 is wrong and in fact needs correction. I know that the letter has caused wrong impressions among members who have come to me and inquired as to the position the Mennonite Church took in its stand against abolition of capital punishment.
On April 23 I received a letter from Reverend R. J. Scott, who is the secretary to the task force on the abolition of capital punishment for the Canadian Council of Churches. He wrote in part, after first stating that he had not received my letter:
Our reference to the Mennonite Church may have been inaccurate in view of your reference to the different independent sections of the Mennonite Church. We included the name in our list as we had a representative on our Committee from the Mennonite Central Committee, Kitchener, Ontario. We were not aware of other groupings.
So the wrong impression has been created.
In his speech on May 19, 1976, as reported at page 13681 of Hansard, the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) used the argument that among other churches the Mennonite has also spoken out in favour of the abolition of capital punishment. But he made what I imagine was an innocent mistake, because although there are a number of denominations in our background he used the following words:
Capital Punishment
I think of a wonderful statement by the Mennonite Brethren-
He continued:
-who are convinced abolitionists and who, at the risk of worrying those who profess to be followers, make clear and unequivocal statements in favour of abolition.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I happen to be a member of the denomination about which the hon. member speaks. He was confused in that our denomination never passed a resolution. We are debating that resolution now, so, unhappily the wrong impression has been created by the press releases which have been brought before the public by the Canadian Council of Churches.
As I say, I do not question the abolitionist stand that such a person has an honest conscience. However, I think it should be very clearly pointed out for the record that what some people take to be facts are in fact not facts at all. The main issue for me, and I imagine for many other members of this House, is a moral one. All of us have already heard the quotation from Genesis 9:6. The quotation "thou shalt not kill" raises the question: are we justified in taking a human life? Are we justified in taking the life of another human being in judgment for the crime he or she may have committed?
Quite frankly I cannot accept the humanistic view of society which seems to argue that man from his own position, from his own innate goodness, can inject a will to do good. I cannot accept that. We are agents of a free will; but the very fact that we are debating this subject today gives mute evidence to the fact that man is exceedingly wicked and that man does not stop at anything in respect of raising his hand against his brother. I do not think any of us should be so smug or complacent that we feel we are exempt from that possibility.
It is true that in our present society there are many countervailing forces which, to my mind, debase society. I need only mention the violence on television. This is a medium which affects virtually every Canadian. Day after day violence is pumped into the homes of Canadians to the point where it seems almost to take on real life at tributes for many Canadians. We have seen a tremendous increase in pornographic material of various kinds. I submit all this diminishes the moral fabric of society.
I do not wish to sound as being holier than thou, but I think it is important to place before this House and the people of Canada the suggestion that if society is to survive it will survive only if it accepts a moral basis for its existence. While I realize that as a legislator one cannot legislate morality, I do not accept the argument that one cannot show moral leadership. In fact I believe it is our responsibility, so I reject the so-called permissive or humanistic society in which every man is allowed to do his own thing, the only qualification being so long as it does not hurt someone else, because then it is no business of yours or mine. The fact that we are brothers precludes a situation in which the actions I take would not in some form or another affect if not the major society of which I am a member, the closest society in which I am intimately involved.
Many social engineers today seem to think that by behavioural changes, in one form or another, society will
13956

May 28, 1976
Capital Punishment
almost attain a Utopian quality. That just is not the case. I realize that in the Old Testament many crimes are mentioned for which capital punishment was prescribed, and therefore the argument is made that if that be the case in respect of the Old Testament why should it not be prescribed for present society if we are to use Biblical quotations. I have also heard the argument of people who say that because of the New Testament we do not now live under the law, that we now live in a period of grace. That is true. They argue that because it is a fact we live in a period of grace the death penalty no longer is necessary, because we are creatures who have a high regard for human life. But, Mr. Speaker, although the God is a God of grace and love he did not lose the attributes of justice or holiness. He retained those attributes. Today the state is God's agent in making sure that people in today's society can in fact live out their lives in peace and harmony, so the state has a responsibility well beyond that of the individual.
It is not right for me as an individual to ask for retribution, an eye for an eye or a tooth for a tooth, but the state has another role because we must keep in mind that setting the brakes on law drags down everyone in society. In fact in the Old Testament there are references to the fact that crime pollutes the land. Judgment and punishment are not retributive. Punishment must follow actions in which God's laws are broken. We hear so much, for example, of Romans Chapter XII in which the Apostle Paul speaks of the God of Love, the God who is willing to bless his people, the God of forgiveness; but so often we do not read on to the early verses of Chapter XIII in which the same apostle writes:
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers- namely, the government.
it is there by God's appointment. So those who refuse to obey the laws of the land are refusing to obey God, and punishment will follow. For civil authorities do not frighten those who are doing right, but those who are doing wrong. The government is the agent of God for your good. But if you do evil, you should be afraid. For the civil authority does not bear and wear the sword for nothing. It is God's agent to execute his punishment and vengeance on the wrongdoer.
I know reference has been made in the House to the crucifixion story. As we recall, there were two malefactors who were crucified with Christ, one rejected the salvation, the other one did not. But what is significant is that Christ did not offer physical salvation from pain of death but today he offers spiritual salvation. So while I would like to live in a society where punishment is not necessary, where reconciliation of man and his God can take place, that is not the society in which I live. I must finally come to the conclusion that the state is an agent of God, responsible to him to see that justice is carried out and that those who obey the laws of the country are in fact protected. It is on that basis that I cannot support Bill C-84.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second occasion since 1972 that I participate in a debate on capital punishment. I would like to say at the outset that I am a retentionist. I believed in capital punishment before I came to Ottawa, I spoke in favour of it in the 1972 and 1974 election campaigns, and my position has not changed.

Despite the fact that the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) says that capital punishment is not a deterrent, I firmly believe it is. The Solicitor General referred to various statistics and suggested that they are conclusively in favour of the fact that capital punishment is not a deterrent. I have examined these statistics and I suggest they can be used either way. If you an abolitionist you can use the statistics to support your argument, and if you are a retentionist you can use them for the same purpose.
The Solicitor General in the debate on this subject on May 3, as recorded at page 13089 of Hansard, said the following:
The burden of proof is on those who propose retention of the death penalty. They must show that retention does some good in society and has positive effect. Furthermore, I do not think retentionists can logically or ethically discharge that burden of truth.
I find that statement rather illogical. Why should the burden of proof be on the retentionist and not on the abolitionist? What the minister is saying is simply that he is right and the rest of us are wrong, and he will be right unless we can prove that he is wrong.
In March of 1975 the Solicitor General sent out a document entitled, "The Prevention and Control of Violent Crime in Canada: Some Comments on Violent Crime, Capital Punishment and Other Related Issues". At page 5 of this document we find the following statement:
One or more of the following factors are usually present:-
He is referring to murder.
-quarrels or a history of quarrels between friends and family members; situations where alcohol or drugs are present; situations where immediate access to firearms exists, situations where the eventual offender feels threatened by others present in the situation, and cases of mental or emotional instability and derangement. Given the sudden, unplanned nature of most homicide it appears unlikely that most individuals who commit murder take into account the existence or non-existence of capital punishment before carrying out the act.
The Solicitor General is not really being fair when he makes that statement because the type of killings he refers to in this paper do not and never have called for capital punishment. Generally speaking they have called for life imprisonment or imprisonment for a period of time. These killings to which he refers are not premeditated murders, and I believe that 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the public according to the polls, and some 87 per cent of the people in my constituency believe in capital punishment for premeditated murder. They are not calling for capital punishment in situations such as were described by the Solicitor General.
I believe that in instances of planned murder, in cases of contract murder, and in cases of killings during the commission of a crime, capital punishment is a deterrent because in these particular situations the individual is fully aware ahead of time what he is doing. If he goes into a bank to rob it and takes a gun with him, he knows perfectly well that the circumstances may be such that he will use that gun. What I am suggesting is that if the individual is aware of the fact that because of his action he might have to face capital punishment, that is certainly a deterrent.
To some people capital punishment is abhorrent. I listened the other day to a member on the other side of the House when he described a hanging in some detail, sug-
May 28, 1976

gesting it was cruel, bloodthirsty, and revengeful. But he did not look at the other side of the coin; he did not consider the terror experienced by the victim, nor did he consider the heartbreak and the effect of a killing on the victim's family. I suggest to that particular member that he talk to members of a family who have lost someone in a killing, as I have. He would have second thoughts, I am certain. If his argument is simply that he is opposed to the particular method of capital punishment, hanging, I would suggest that this is not a valid argument for an abolitionist. The answer is that that particular individual should press for changes in the law which will provide for a different method of execution, for example, the injection of a drug or the giving of some particular type of poison by putting it in the guilty person's food.
In the same report put out by the Solicitor General in March, 1975, to which I already referred, the minister had this to say:
The commandment, "Thou shalt not kill" is part of our Judaeo-Chris-tian heritage. It emphasizes the value of human life and should make us ponder whether we should take yet another life in retribution.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), who preceded me, discussed the religious aspect in some detail. Over the past four years I have received a great deal of correspondence on the subject of capital punishment, and much of this correspondence has come to me from religious organizations, the Council of Churches, and individuals who have religious backgrounds who have made studies of the Bible. It is very interesting to note that the theologians themselves are divided on the interpretation of the Bible as it refers to capital punishment. It is interesting to note that both sides make use of quotations from the Bible to support their argument for or against, but a few days ago I was interested to receive in the mail a bit of correspondence which indicated to me that the American Revised Standard Version of the Bible in translating from the original, rather than saying "thou shalt not kill" says "thou shalt not murder." In other words there is a distinction between the act of killing and the act of murder.
A short time ago I had occasion to read an article in one of the Toronto newspapers written by a rabbi of the Jewish faith. It was referred to by the hon. member for Provencher, and I was impressed by that article. It went into some detail and gave arguments both pro and con. In summing it up the rabbi said that he himself believed in the abolition of capital punishment, but I found the final sentence in the article very interesting because he concluded by saying, "Who is to say that I am right and you are wrong?"
Finally, I say this to the abolitionists: because one is a retentionist does not mean that he is cruel, coldblooded, hardhearted or has utter and complete disregard for human life. I suggest that it is much easier to be an abolitionist than it is to be a retentionist because, if capital punishment is retained, when an execution does take place each of us who has voted in favour of retaining capital punishment must bear part of the responsibility for the carrying out of that execution.
May I call it four o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL OFFICE OF EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which I am prepared to debate this afternoon calls for the government to consider the establishment of a national office of education. Maybe I should first explain the aspects of the current situation in education that led me to consider the need for a national office.
When I was first elected to this House in 1973 I introduced this motion, and again in 1974 when I was re-elected. Having come from a background of education I felt there was need for such an office. As you know, Mr. Speaker, education is primarily a provincial matter, but several federal departments are involved in educational schemes. The Department of the Secretary of State funds much of the post-secondary education in Canada. All government concerns are facing a strong financial squeeze at precisely the same time that we have reached a watershed period in education. At the same time that governments are cutting education budgets there is a questioning among educators, students, and parents about where education should go. There is no national focus on this question nor has a national defender come out in defence of education budgets.
We have just finished a major expansion of post-secondary education to the point that we now have over 600,000 students in colleges and universities. Secondary school enrollments have expanded to include a greater proportion of the age group and a far greater total population as the baby boom passed through the system; vocational education has mushroomed.
The system will have fewer students after the baby boom and there may have to be cutbacks. Meantime there is a widespread questioning of educational goals in Canada ranging from those who want to see the return of the three Rs to those who still want to implement the free spirit of the individual and creativity of the Hall-Denis report in Ontario as set out in "Living and Learning".
Recently several perennial problems have occurred that still must be faced and solved. Regional barriers to good education still exist; economic barriers abound, and equity demands that these be removed.
When I began teaching in 1957 the community I was in experienced great mobility. I was amazed to learn that

when students came from the east coast, for instance, to Ontario their grade VI was not evaluated in the same light in Ontario. The reason given was that their curricula were not the same as those of Ontario. Teacher training was not co-ordinated and teachers coming into Ontario were not accepted on par with Ontario-graduated teachers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL OFFICE OF EDUCATION
speechtext: And vice-versa.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL OFFICE OF EDUCATION
speechtext:
Exactly. Out of all these considerations came a judgment that a national office is necessary to focus attention on this national issue and to provide coordination and information to a national debate on these issues.
I should like to explain some of the details of the motion before the House this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. One might ask why the federal government should get involved. I have already said that this is a national issue. To those who say that the federal government has no jurisdiction or interest I would point out that the federal government is already involved in several ways through the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Department of the Secretary of State, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Department of National Defence, the Department of External Affairs, CIDA, the National Museums, the National Library and Public Archives, the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of the Solicitor General, and the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Let us not kid ourselves that we are not already into it up to our necks.
We hide behind the facade that the federal government has no place in education, but we are certainly involved in terms of finance, training programs, and upgrading programs.
The recent OECD report on Canadian education estimated that over 20 per cent of all expenditures on education come from the federal government. I am not arguing that we should immediately get into it more deeply, but primarily that we should establish a national office to allow the provinces, the educators, and ourselves to make more co-ordinated decisions about the future education of our children. If we do not have this co-ordination on a national level the education questions of direction and budget will be decided willy-nilly in over ten different bureaucracies across the country.
Incredible as it seems to non-Canadians who visit Canada, we do not have a national office to administer even the minimal dissemination and collation of research into education. The result is often a tragic ignorance in one province about what goes on next door. The result is also major knowledge gaps for planners. What is the demand for adult training going to be in ten years so that we can plan for it? No one has the answer. What is the critical age at which economic disparity will lead to decisions to curtail education in a student's mind? We do not know. But we do know that in poor working class areas the number of high schools per capita is much lower than in affluent areas, and that the proportion of age groups in school varies greatly. What are the implications for vocational schools if more students attend regular high schools? What are the job training needs that we must anticipate for 15 years from now?
May 28, 1976

Without national co-ordination of the effort to collect and disseminate basic information, decisions will continue to be made in ignorance of future trends and possible solutions that are being tried in other parts of the country.
Similarly I have recommended in this motion that the national office arrange for staff and students to travel to other parts of the country to learn first-hand about the practices outside their own areas.
The third function of the national education office would be to focus the contribution we make towards improving educational opportunities in the Third World. At present we have students applying from these countries to universities and colleges in every province, facing a variety of different educational requirements and offerings. At the same time our federal agencies work with the countries concerned to assist them in improving the level of education of their students and, ultimately, their society. The provinces take no part in this nor do they assist the federal government in determining which programs are more suitable, or in providing financing for those students. So we have the recent situation where Ontario announced an increase of fees for students on visas at the same time that the federal government is trying to increase the number of students from abroad for training in our universities.
Finally, the education office could act as a channel for bringing educational issues to the attention of the Council of Ministers of Education of the provinces. I have said earlier that I believe that the discussion of the educational goals for our country is essential, that it is of immediate concern, and that it must be done nationally to be most effective and equitable. It is my hope that by bringing the issues to the ministers they would be encouraged to discuss them more seriously and more frequently than they have up to the present.
It seems to me, for example, there is a need to set some kind of national goals for education. One major example is the whole question of bilingualism. Recently we had the Director of Official Languages, Mr. Keith Spicer, telling us that we should have started with the schools. Mr. Speaker, that is one very obvious area. Parliament having adopted a national policy of bilingualism, it seemed to me and many Canadians that the best place to have began implementing that program was in the school system. If bilingualism is to be a national goal, a federal office of education ought to provide national direction. One of the great short-comings of the present program lies in the lack of such direction. The lack of national direction has hampered considerably our efforts with respect to bilingualism.
It seems to me that if we bring this issue to the attention of the ministers of education, through a national office of education, we could encourage more frequent and wide-ranging discussions of the subject; hopefully, provinces could co-ordinate their actions. Hopefully our aims in education could be co-ordinated and provincial hopes fulfilled. Without a national office to co-ordinate the collection of such information and to arrange that the appropriate material is circulated to those who need it, I believe decisions will continue to be made in isolation from these national goals.
Education
Notice, Mr. Speaker, that my proposal calls for coordinating and encouraging the dissemination of educational information. You will notice that it would provide the national education office with no real powers apart from the ones I suggested. In truth I should like to see a stronger office. This will not be possible unless the provinces wish to strengthen their role in the field. I see the establishment of this national office as a first small step. Establishing this office would establish a body which can ensure that discussion proceeds on the basis of proper information. The office could act as a catalyst to stimulate discussion. It would go no further without the willing co-operation of the provinces, and could not go much further owing to the limited jurisdiction of the federal government in this field.
As I say, I see the establishment of such an office as a first step. Hopefully we could proceed beyond that stage in terms of a national educational policy. Some, I know, feel that the establishment of this body would be beyond the scope of section 93 of the British North America Act, but such people ignore the major role the federal government already plays in the field. Its activities go far beyond the degree of involvement proposed in the motion before the House. I therefore suggest that any who say the federal government should not set up a national educational office are hiding behind what I call the flim-flammery of the constitution, particularly section 93.
My view that the constitution is not a block to the setting up of a national education office or policy in the field of federal action is supported by the constitutional authority, Mr. J. A. Corry. He has stated:
... so whatever the dilemma about education in the Canadian federation is, it is not a constitutional one. Indeed s.93 becomes a model of flexibility. Whenever it becomes clear that special educational provision is needed to carry out responsibilities undertaken by parliament in the exercise of its exclusive powers in section 91, parliament is entitled to manage that provision by whatever means and instrumentalities are required in the circumstances. As so often turns out in this country, obstacles to action that are declared to be formidable constitutional barriers turn out to be merely political.
Our children and their education are too important to be played with politically. Until we treat education as a national priority and work with the provinces to eliminate national disparities, economic barriers to educational advancement, poor distribution of resources, ignorance of new advances, and fear and confusion in the discussion of educational goals there will be no solution of the problem. Not until we stop treating education as a tool of an economic stabilization policy will it be given the high priority it deserves in our cultural and social priorities. I hope that the formation of a national office will allow the provinces and federal government to do something they have never done before in the absence of a national focus on these issues, think in terms wider rather than narrow jurisdictions about the real educational issues which face us now and will face us in the future.
Finally, I hope the next time an international team of experts evaluates our education they will not be able to say, as was said in a recent OECD report, that:
Canada has trodden down its own path with an array of exceptionally active programs for quantitative expansion and significant qualitative change of education systems that are however derived from no explicitly stated over-all national conception of the country's interests . .. The general tone of (provincial) policy-making appears to be adaptations to

May 28, 1976
Education
short-term pressures doing a little more than what already has been done and above all pressing for economies and reductions of expenditures.
I hope government members will not talk out this motion but accept what it represents, the initial, official federal thrust in this area, a thrust which will be given recognition by the establishment of the particular office alluded to in the motion.
I do not make my comments in isolation. The Canadian Teachers Federation, which represents a federated body of teachers right across this country, since 1971 has consistently recommended to the federal government the establishment of an office along the lines outlined in the motion now before the House, Indeed not only the Canadian Teachers Federation supports such an office; the Canadian Trustees Association, an association of school trustees of this country, has also urged the government to move in this direction.
Surely, if we concede that in a democracy the people ought to have some say in these matters, if we concede that there ought to be some dialogue, then the group which is elected to represent the best interests of education in the country ought to carry some weight with the government. Surely their attitude ought to indicate to the government their willingness to work actively within the kind of framework suggested this afternoon.
As I say, I hope hon. members opposite will not talk out this motion but, instead, accept its concept and let it come to a vote. Let us set about the business of establishing national goals in education in this country.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL OFFICE OF EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to speak on the motion proposed by the hon. member on my extreme left. I was once a member of the Canadian Teachers Federation. In my relatively early youth I became a member of the Canadian Trustees Association. Now, of course, I am in that most omniscient of all groups, the parents of the products of our educational institutions.
The hon. member is to be commended for bringing forward a suggestion that is reasonable, reasoned, and timely. If I may say so, I think he was wise to discuss a national office rather than a national department. As he points out, to suggest the establishment of a national department might involve too direct an attack on well-established constitutional principles and patterns. I believe that much can be gained if there is a more informed, active, and

uplifting role on the part of the national level of government in the important field of education.
The strengthening of national ideals and national purpose surely involves the educational process most heavily. The one level of government whose goals are national, not regional, not provincial, and not local, surely must be and is indeed the national government.
It is clear that much has happened since those years when we assumed from the provisions of the British North America Act that education was solely and purely a responsibility and function of the provincial jurisdiction. Federal presence has been felt in many, many ways in education, and nearly always in beneficial ways.
I believe that the university grants established, if I remember right, under the Prime Ministership of Mr. St. Laurent were one of the most forward steps ever taken by a national government. Who can say how many universities and how many thousands of university students were enabled to obtain a better life through that move, which was regarded by some of that time as an improper invasion of provincial jurisdiction? I am convinced that nothing but good came from that initiative.
If we look at the matter carefully we see that the federal presence, the federal fiscal presence in particular, is omnipresent. How many of our scholars depend upon assistance which emanates from Ottawa? How much research is encouraged from Ottawa? Indeed it is our claim that there has been a diminution in the national contribution to this important field.
I agree profoundly with the hon. member when he directed our attention to the role of our young people in the international scene and vice-versa. It is a matter of most profound concern that Canada and its educational institutions should be open to the young people of the world. We should encourage young people from different cultures to come and participate with our young people in the learning process. I suppose one of the most worthwhile endeavours in the last generation is the activity of the CUSO program-excellent ambassadors of this country, a world contribution to what one might call the Canadian outreach abroad.
I agree too with a view that is now becoming acceptable; that in the whole question of language training we must begin at the elementary school. There were many who thought that the report of the Commissioner of Official Languages was breaking new ground in his recent report. However, it was a quarter of a century ago that one of the greatest Canadians, Dr. Wilder Penfield, with his great learning and scientific and medical background, suggested exactly the same thing. Therefore this aspect of the hon. member's argument commends itself to me most strongly.
I think that it would be better to have an even stronger presence than he suggests, but I am pragmatic on this which shows that both Conservatives and socialists can be pragmatic if they put their minds to it. If they want to accomplish things, it is just as well that they both do.
I am never given to long speeches. I think that brevity is the soul of wit, as a great man once said. I will simply say that this is a positive contribution. It is the kind of subject
May 28, 1976

that our national parliament, on a sunny Friday afternoon, should be directing its thought and attention to. I commend the hon. member for his initiative and the well reasoned presentation with which he brought it forward.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL OFFICE OF EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by saying that the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) has done a service by raising for discussion the matter of the federal presence in education.
I am not sure that the national office of education which the hon. member proposes would, in fact, do anything which is not now being done by the education support branch of the Secretary of State. I also think that the establishment of such an office might be perceived by the provinces as a direct assumption of their responsibilities as opposed to the collaborative sharing of responsibilities that now occurs in the field of education.
I think that the discussion of federal-provincial roles in education is very timely, particularly in view of the fact that the Fiscal Arrangements Act is due for review and that letters from the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) to the ten provincial ministers of education were tabled in this House yesterday. I hope, therefore, that today's discussion will be useful in this broad consideration of the federal role in education.
The Secretary of State, in a speech in Toronto in March, 1974, said:
One of the dangers of the current attention being focused on federal-provincial relations is that it makes for such sensational copy. As so often happens, the debate that rages around some initial question eventually comes to obscure that question altogether. Our attention is turned from what we are fighting for (if that is not too belligerent a term) to the fighting itself, and we as a nation can ill-afford to pay the social and political costs which such recklessness must surely entail.
The motion before us today allows us an opportunity to consider in a dispassionate way some of the arguments for or against direct federal involvement in education; the non-partisan atmosphere of private member's hour may assist us in assessing alternatives and trying to arrive at solutions on the ground of what Aristotle called "reason free from passion".
In the history of federal-provincial relations, education has been a central concern for a long time. The British North America Act of 1867 defined legislative jurisdiction over education "in and for each province" as exclusively a provincial matter. But the Fathers of Confederation could not anticipate the changes in education-both adult and childhood education, part-time and full-time-needed to deal with technological and other changes in the last century.
What the Fathers of Confederation did realize, however, was that the unity of our nation might not infrequently be subject to stresses and strains, that there was need for vigilance if the federation were to survive, and that the primary responsibility of the federal government was to protect the interest of the nation. In order to respond adequately to the needs of all Canadians the federal and provincial governments developed a continuing working relationship out of which came a series of formal or tacit agreements to deal with specific areas.
Education
It has been said that federation is the most difficult and inefficient of all forms of government, that every time attempts are made to reach agreements our national strength of purpose is tested more or less severely. However, in our great nation there are very great regional differences and, while the effort to reconcile differences is often difficult, it is also true that as a nation we have learned a good deal about reconciling differences and working together in ways that use our collective energies most productively. The task of establishing in Canada an education system which will enable Canadians to respond creatively to the demands of the present and of the future is a task which calls for the fullest and most effective use of those energies.
Although the terms of the BNA Act of 1867 defined education as a provincial responsibility, direct federal support came quickly, beginning in 1874 with the creation of the Royal Military College. The Agricultural Instruction Act of 1913 similarly applied federal moneys to specific educational purposes. During World War I the federal government of the time recognized that a national research effort would be essential for post-war development of Canadian industry and the growth of the national economy and in 1916 the National Research Council was created, although it was not until the 1930's that the National Research Council set up its own laboratories and began its extensive program of research grants to universities.
With the reduction in provincial expenditures in education during the depression years, universities turned to the federal government with requests for direct financial assistance. The difficulties of the universities elicited in 1940 a sympathetic response from the Rowell-Sirois Commission on Dominion-Provincial Relations which, while re-emphasizing the provincial responsibility for education, recommended small per capita federal grants to universities in order to ensure "equal participation of all regions in the national life". This recommendation was not in fact implemented at that time and universities continued to be largely self-financed and autonomous and increasingly concerned about their ability to survive. With the anticipated post-World War II influx of war veterans into universities the federal government enacted the Veterans Rehabilitation Act of 1945 which provided institutions of post-secondary education with temporary relief only. By 1949 the universities had renewed their appeal for federal funding.
There seem to have been two main issues raised by the universities at that time-the possibility of damage to the country's economy if the universities' financial crisis forced them to reduce the training of professional manpower, and the possibility of raising fees to a level which students from lower income families could not meet, thus threatening the principle of equal opportunity for all Canadians to which the national government has always been committed.
In 1951 the Massey Commission on the National Development of Arts, Letters and Sciences recommended that a small per capita grant of 50 cents be made to the universities, and this recommendation was immediately implemented by the federal government. The Massey Commission, however, was concerned with much more than

May 28, 1976
Education
financial rescue on an ad hoc basis. The preamble to the Commission's terms of reference included the following: "It is in the national interest to give encouragement to institutions which express national feeling, promote common understanding and add to the variety and richness of Canadian life, rural as well as urban". The report recommended continued active involvement on the part of the national government to ensure the cultural and intellectual development of the country as a whole. I quote from that report as follows:
... all civilized societies strive for a common good, including not only material but intellectual and moral elements. If the federal government is to renounce its right to associate itself with other social groups, public and private, in the general education of Canadian citizens, it denies its intellectual and moral purpose, the complete conception of the common good is lost, and Canada, as such, becomes a materialistic society.
Implementation of the recommendations of the Massey Commission from 1951 on saw the federal government develop its current role as patron of arts and culture and patron of education and research.
The activities of such national institutions as the CBC, the National Film Board, and the Canada Council represent part of the federal involvement in education in the broad sense of the word. The activities of the Medical Research Council and the National Research Council are two examples of more specific clearly defined efforts to ensure the advancement of knowledge and the development of Canadian technology.
Adult education has been supported by the federal government in a variety of ways for a long time-grants to such organizations as Frontier College, the Canadian Association for Adult Education, the training grants administered through the Department of Manpower in collaboration with the provinces, are all part of the continuing effort to provide Canadians with education and training appropriate to a variety of situations and needs.
In 1966 the Secretary of State was assigned the task of advising cabinet on post-secondary education, and an education support branch was established in that department. It later became responsible for the administration of that part of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act of 1967 which relates to post-secondary education.
In 1973 the Department of the Secretary of State was designated by cabinet as the agency within the federal government responsible for co-ordinated development, formulation, implementation and review of federal policies and programs relating to education. The responsibilities of the branch are broad and appear to me to include all the functions which the hon. member for Nickel Belt proposes for a national office of education. Areas in which the branch now has responsibilities include:
1.	Federal policies and programs in support of postsecondary education generally;
2.	Communication with provincial governments, the academic community and national organizations on matters of education;
3.	Co-operating with the Department of External Affairs in co-ordination of Canada's effective participation in international fora on educational questions;
4.	Evaluating the effectiveness of federal policies and programs in support of education against national goals.

Among other activities the staff of the branch participated in the OECD review of education policies in Canada and the preparation of a federal-provincial report entitled Education in Canada for the International Bureau of Education-UNESCO. I shall refer later to that UNESCO document which raises exciting new prospectives in education.
In the international field the staff of the branch have participated with Department of External Affairs officials in meetings of major international organizations and agencies-OECD,	UNESCO and the Commonwealth
Secretariat. The branch was represented on Canadian delegations to the OECD Education Committee and the Biennial Conference of the International Bureau of Education- UNESCO-as well as in preparations for the Commonwealth Conference on Educational Broadcasting.
At the present time one hears two conflicting opinions on the issue of direct national or federal involvement in education. The Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, for instance, has claimed that ".. . national involvement of Canadian universities requires a federal presence ... " and, "The universities wish to deal directly with the federal government in matters of national interest". The Canadian Association of University Teachers has expressed a concern at the current tendency to view postsecondary education from a purely regional perspective, arguing that a wider viewpoint is necessary if universities are to be allowed to make their full contribution to Canadian life. On the other hand provincial governments are now seeking to play a greater role in the distribution of educational moneys. In times of restraint, questions of priorities and resource allocation arise, and educational objectives that were largely unexamined during the period of unrestrained growth are now being questioned and re-evaluated. We probably had unrealistic expectations of education, but certain there is a fairly high degree of disillusionment in the country because education has not provided a better social and political order and the realisation of many ideals.
Because education enjoys so large a proportion of public funds there is increased concern about accountability. The Fiscal Arrangements Act of 1967 ties federal contributions for post-secondary education to the operating expenditures of each institution which, in turn, are dependent on the allocation of provincial resources. This means, in effect, that certain provincial disparities in the provision of postsecondary education across Canada continue and this is certainly an area that should be examined in anticipation of the expiry of the present arrangements in 1977.
Apart from the federal government's concern about equality of opportunity for Canadians, the federal government also has a particular interest in education, particularly in post-secondary education in terms of preparation for the job market. It is the national government that has the responsibility for keeping in view the manpower needs of the whole nation. Since 1964 the Canada Student Loans Plan has represented an important source of assistance to provide Canadians with equality of opportunity to further their career goals.
The UNESCO report to which I referred earlier, published in 1972 and entitled "Learning to be", suggested a
May 28, 1976

very radical transition in our traditional views on education. Modern technology, it suggests, has made the mere aquisition of information the function of the computer and has released man from the routine of mental labour. In the light of these advances the report claims that "liberating the energies of the people, unleasing their creative power, heads the list of future prospects for the development of education in the world of tomorrow." Demographic changes in Canada will impose other changes in education. As future populations include fewer children and proportionately more adults who may need to retrain and re-adapt a number of times in their career lives, changes become implicit in childhood as well as in post-secondary education, if, the words of the UNESCO report, people are to "learn to live, learn to learn, so as to be able to absorb new knowledge all through life, learn to think freely and critically; learn to love the world and to make it more human".
As we approach this exciting and difficult task I think that the solutions will be found, not in establishing one new agency as the motion before us proposes, but rather in a very sensitive working out of formulas which neither infringe on provincial jurisdiction nor deny the responsibility of the national government in this area.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL OFFICE OF EDUCATION
