Mr. Speaker, I too would like to congratulate the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) on his excellent recitation. Unfortunately, while I find it intellectually extremely timely, because of our present restraints program I think it is hardly economically feasible, and this I regret very much. However, I am so enthused by many of his thoughts that I might suggest that this be put on our agenda for our post-AIB controls program.
I should like to refer to some of the points he made with which I thoroughly agree. He spoke or the unequal educational opportunities that exist for the youth across Canada. This is a fear that haunts every concerned parent in this country. Is a child who has to move from one province to another, especially during mid-term, going to have equal opportunity because of the move? It is not only moving from one province to another; it is also moving from one board of education to another. The riding that I have the honour to represent has two different boards of education, each with quite a different system. If a child moves just three blocks away in the same city, he goes to a different system of education with different opportunities offered. As I say, this is a fear that haunts parents.
The hon. member also referred to the long-term demands of the labour market. This too is of extreme importance. It is often foolhardy, even cruel, of us to insist that youngsters stay in school and become highly educated, only to have them pushed into intellectually bankrupt jobs. Then there are questions like job satisfaction, pride is one's activity, and so on. Which of us at this moment would dare criticize the youth of this country because they are dissatisfied with their jobs, since we have not prepared them perhaps for the right job? We just tell them to get educated; we do not have the foresight to proper jobs.
The hon. member also mentioned national goals. Obviously bilingualism should receive high priority. I should like to mention some of my own priorities. For instance, Canadian studies. I should like to refer the House to a test
Education
that was conducted, I believe last year, by Mel Hurtig among 3,500 final year high school students across Canada. It was quite a simple test on Canadianism, yet 62 per cent of those students failed and 61 per cent did not even know that the British North America Act is the Constitution of Canada. Many of these students believed that Toronto or Montreal was the capital of Canada. After receiving the results of his test, one student said, "After going through this I found myself wondering what it was that I had learned in 13 years of school". Another said, "I can't believe how ignorant I am about Canada".
Is it not reasonable to expect that Canadian children should be learning elementary facts about their country in Canadian schools? A research group at Glendon College, York University, showed that only one third of Canadian schools surveyed had courses in Canadian literature.
As for the matter of text books, a study by the Independent Publishers' Association of Canada shows that 88 per cent of school library money goes to foreign books. Some Canadian school boards spend every cent of their money in the United States. What I am preaching is not narrowminded nationalism; I am asking that Canadian children should have some knowledge of this country and its history, how government works, world issues and how they affect Canada. They should be taught pride in Canada, and concern for its survival as an independent country. Our children should be taught concern for the rich multicultural heritage that Canada enjoys. Here again, why is it that only children lucky enough to live in the bigger centres of Canada can really appreciate the rich multicultural heritage that is now ours?
How many Canadian children know about native rights? How many of them know how our native people live and what their aspirations are? As I said, these are some points that personally I should like to see added to this list of things to which an office such as the hon. member suggests could dedicate itself.
Coming back to the subject of textbooks I shall quote from the "Canadian Journal of Studies" for May, 1975, a statement by William Clarke, President of Clarke-Irwin & Co. Limited:
While the federal government may not have direct involvement in the process of determining curriculi, the federal government of course is directly involved in many aspects of education through grants to provincial governments for French language instruction, metric conversion and so on, and of course the federal government has a role to play in stimulating if nothing else the creation of Canadian educational material in co-operation with provincial governments. This is a role which is desperately needed.
I first became interested in the question of federal cooperation, shall we say, in education in our country when I received a letter shortly after my election in 1974 from the Canadian School Trustees' Association. One paragraph of this letter reads as follows:
.. . we believe that there is a national context to education; one that must be recognized to a far greater degree than at present if we want students in all schools of Canada to be able to compete on equal terms for the good life this country can provide. We further believe that recognition of the national context of education can be given without offence to the British North America Act.

I am not a constitutional expert and therefore I do not intend to go into those aspects. It is interesting, however, to note that further to my expression of interest the Canadian School Trustees' Association further elaborated their aims and objects. They state:
The values are as follows:
1.	There is a growing national complex to education in this country. It requires a recognizeable office of the federal government to assist in the co-ordination:
a) national objectives whereby we want the children of Canada to become Canadians and not Alberta Canadians, Quebec Canadians, Ontario Canadians, etc.
(b)	levels of equivalencies whereby parents can move from one province to another and feel assured that their children will encounter educational requirements that are similar from one grade to another.
(c)	assistance in the co-ordinating and effective use of the newer media available, especially in programs that can be used in any one province at any time. There is not only a need for materials to use in the newer media, but also for effective methods of distribution.
(d)	there is a need to develop instructional technology that school boards can use in any province.
(e)	bilingualism is a fact of life in Canada now, but the children in the schools must be prepared for a bilingual Canada in terms of cultural values, and in terms of competing for employment. There is a need to provide for some co-ordinating agency, and instructional materials that are effective and quick.
(f)	leadership and co-ordination in all facets of education.
(g)	Canada is really handicapped in its communications with other countries who have federal offices of education of various kinds. We need to be equipped with an office that can speak for Canada in educational matters at UNESCO, OECD and other international meetings.
(h)	there is not equality of opportunity to education in Canada at the present time, despite many attempts to provide same. If Canada is to be one country from sea-to-sea, the children in this country must have such equality of opportunity. The parochialism of Canada needs to be tempered considerably, and an Office of Education in Ottawa could assist materially in such matters.
2.	There are constitutional problems that inhibit the formation of an Office of Education-but such problems have not presented the massive
sums of money that the federal government contributes to post-secondary education. The provinces agree to the federal government being involved, in fact are seeking more involvement in financial terms at the post-secondary level. There is no reason why such co-operation could not be developed in the interests of Canadian children who are entitled to inherit a country that is Canadian first.
3.	Federal government policies, especially in programs that require contributions from the provinces, affect the over-all budgets in the provinces, and hence the budgets for the provincial departments of education. There is no office in Ottawa at the present time to remind the federal government that social programs of cost-sharing nature will affect educational resources both financial and human. The situation has grown to the point where we feel that there must be an official office in Canada to speak for education and protect its interests in every part of Canada.
4.	There is also a very great need for research and development of education in Canada, and we have just witnessed the cancellation of an educational technology department which was doing valuable work in giving counsel and leadership to education in such matters as audiovisual aides, videodiscs, computer assisted learning etc. If there had been an Office of Education the cancellation could have been averted.
5.	Generally speaking, we are a growing nation that needs to have a well prepared generation to take over-a generation that will be understanding, co-operative and compassionate to the very great diversities of this country in cultures and languages. Without leadership in such matters through an Office of Education the requirement is not being adequately met. The future of this country calls for such an office.
6.	The Secretary of State is involved to a great degree in education, and the work being done by him is appreciated-but more is necessary-the Secretary of State has many matters of concern. The fact that the Secretary of State is in education, with the consent of the provinces, is a strong argument in favour of a national office.
The fact that the ministers of education in Canada have formed the Council of Ministers of Education/Canada is another strong argument-there was a need, and they are trying to fill the need.
